title: Sauna and Alcohol: Is It Safe? Risks, Timing and Hot Tubs
excerpt: Is it safe to use a sauna, steam room, or hot tub after drinking? Why heat and alcohol clash, how long to wait, the next-morning hangover sauna, and warning signs.
metaDescription: Is a sauna or hot tub safe after drinking? Why heat and alcohol clash, how long to wait, whether you can sweat out a hangover, and warning signs to know.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** using a sauna, steam room, or hot tub while you've been drinking is genuinely risky, and it's one of the few everyday combinations that regularly shows up in coroners' reports. Heat and alcohol both widen your blood vessels, both pull your blood pressure down, and both dry you out. Alcohol also dulls the warning signals that would normally tell you to get out. Put together, that can mean fainting, falling, overheating, an abnormal heart rhythm, or, in a hot tub, drowning. One small drink a while before a short session is a very different thing from a few beers in a 90°C sauna, but the safest rule is simple: **if you can feel the drinks, skip the heat.**

**The quick rules:** Don't drink in the sauna or hot tub, and don't go in while you're still feeling the alcohol. Wait until you're fully sober, which for most people means at least an hour per standard drink, and longer after a big night. Never use a sauna or hot tub alone after drinking. If you do go in later, keep it short, drink water before and after, and get out at the first sign of dizziness, nausea, a pounding heart, or a headache. The next-morning "sweat out the hangover" sauna is covered below, and the short version is that it doesn't remove alcohol and can make dehydration worse.

> **When to get help right away.** This is general information, not medical advice. Call 911 (or your local emergency number) if someone who has been drinking in or after a sauna, steam room, or hot tub faints and doesn't come round quickly, is confused or hard to wake, has chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat that won't settle, trouble breathing, a seizure, or has slipped under water even briefly. Get them out of the heat, lay them down somewhere cool, and don't leave them alone. **Talk to your doctor before combining alcohol and heat** if you have heart disease, an irregular heartbeat, low or high blood pressure, epilepsy, diabetes, are pregnant, or take medicines for blood pressure, heart conditions, or mood.

## Why Saunas and Alcohol Are a Bad Mix: What Happens in Your Body

A sauna is a deliberate heat stress. That's part of why people like it. Your skin warms, your heart speeds up, your blood vessels open, and you sweat. In a sober, healthy person those reactions are well controlled. Alcohol interferes with almost every one of them.

### 1. Both open up your blood vessels, so blood pressure drops

To cool you down, your body widens the blood vessels in your skin (this is called vasodilation) and sends more blood toward the surface. That's why you go red in a sauna. Alcohol does the same thing on its own, which is why drinkers get flushed cheeks. Stack the two and a lot of your blood ends up pooled in your skin and legs instead of going to your brain.

Your heart tries to make up for it by beating faster, but there's a limit. The moment you stand up quickly, step out of the hot room, or climb out of a hot tub, gravity pulls even more blood down to your legs. Blood pressure can fall sharply for a few seconds. That's the classic way people faint after a sauna, and alcohol makes it far more likely. A faint is usually brief and harmless on a soft surface. On wet tiles, hot stones, or a stove, it isn't.

### 2. Both dehydrate you

A sauna session can make you sweat a lot, and the amount varies a lot from person to person. Alcohol adds to the problem in a different way: it suppresses a hormone called vasopressin (also known as antidiuretic hormone), which normally tells your kidneys to hold on to water. With less of it, you pee more than you drink. We explain that process in more detail in our guide to [whether alcohol really dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you).

Lower fluid volume means lower blood volume, which feeds straight back into the blood pressure problem above. It also means you lose sodium and potassium in sweat and urine, which can leave you cramping, weak, or lightheaded.

### 3. Alcohol switches off your "get out now" alarm

When you overheat, your body normally sends clear signals: you feel uncomfortable, your head pounds, you feel a strong urge to leave. Alcohol blunts those signals and slows your reaction to them. It also makes you sleepy. That's how people end up staying in far longer than they meant to, or falling asleep in the heat. Alcohol also affects how your body regulates its own temperature, so you can be heating up faster than you realize.

### 4. Your heart is working harder at the same time

Heat makes your heart beat faster. So does alcohol. A heavy drinking session is a known trigger for abnormal heart rhythms, especially atrial fibrillation, a pattern doctors sometimes call "holiday heart" because it shows up after big weekends and holidays. Adding a strong heat load on top of that puts extra strain on a heart that is already being pushed. For most healthy people that means a pounding pulse and feeling rough. For someone with an existing heart problem, it can be dangerous. If you've noticed your [heart racing after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking) before, take that as a reason to be extra careful with heat.

### 5. Judgment and balance go down

This is the unglamorous part. Saunas have hot stoves and hot rocks. Hot tubs have slippery steps and water you can slip under. Alcohol affects balance, coordination, and decision-making, so the risks of burns, falls, and drowning go up. These aren't rare edge cases. They're the most common ways that sauna and hot tub injuries happen.

## What the Evidence Actually Says

There is a lot of good research on saunas, and most of it is positive. Long-running Finnish studies led by Jari Laukkanen and colleagues, including a widely cited 2015 paper in *JAMA Internal Medicine*, found that men who used saunas more often had lower rates of cardiovascular death over the following years. Those were observational studies, so they show a link rather than proof that saunas cause the benefit, but they're a big reason saunas have a healthy reputation.

The same country also has the best data on sauna deaths, and the picture there is consistent. Finnish forensic studies that reviewed deaths in saunas have repeatedly found that alcohol was involved in a large share of them, often in people who were alone and who had been drinking heavily. Finnish public health advice has long been blunt about it: don't mix sauna bathing and alcohol.

For hot tubs, US safety agencies such as the Consumer Product Safety Commission have warned for years against using hot tubs and spas while drinking, because alcohol combined with hot water can cause drowsiness, unconsciousness, and drowning. Separately, alcohol is a well-known factor in adult drownings in general, which is part of why public health bodies like the CDC flag drinking around water as a risk.

What you won't find is a reliable "safe number of drinks" for a sauna. It hasn't been studied in a way that gives a clean threshold, and it would vary a lot with body size, how hot the room is, how long you stay in, and your health. So we're not going to invent one. What the evidence does support is that the danger rises with the amount you've had and how impaired you are, and that being alone makes a bad outcome much more likely.

## Sauna After Drinking: How Long Should You Wait?

There's no official waiting time that fits everyone, but you can work out a sensible one.

Your liver clears alcohol at a fairly steady pace, roughly one standard drink per hour for an average adult, though it varies. Nothing speeds that up much: not coffee, not a cold shower, and not sweating. So a practical guide looks like this:

- **One drink with dinner:** wait at least an hour or two, until you feel completely normal, then keep the session short.
- **Two to four drinks:** wait several hours. If you went out in the evening, that usually means the sauna is a next-day activity, not a nightcap.
- **A big night:** don't use the sauna until the next day, and even then, read the section below on hangovers first.
- **Any time you still feel the drinks** (lightheaded, relaxed, a bit slow), you're not ready. Your feeling of being "fine" is also less reliable after drinking, so err on the side of waiting longer.

When you do go back in, drink a big glass of water first, keep the first round shorter than usual, sit rather than lie down so you notice if you feel faint, and stand up slowly when you leave.

## Drinking in the Sauna: Why the "Sauna Beer" Tradition Is Riskier Than It Looks

In some places, a cold beer in or after the sauna is a cultural tradition, and plenty of people do it without trouble. It's worth understanding why it's riskier than it feels.

Alcohol tends to feel stronger in the heat. You're sweating, slightly dehydrated, and your blood vessels are already wide open, so the same drink can leave you more lightheaded than it would at a table. You're also less likely to notice how much you've had, because a cold drink in a hot room goes down fast.

The second problem is that alcohol is not a hydrating drink. A beer replaces some fluid, but the alcohol in it pushes your kidneys to get rid of more. After a hot session, you need water or something with a bit of salt in it, not more alcohol.

If you're going to have a drink as part of a sauna evening, the safest way is to finish your sauna rounds first, cool down fully, rehydrate with water, and then have your drink, rather than drinking between rounds. If you've had one, call it a night for the sauna.

## Hot Tubs and Alcohol: The Drowning Risk

Hot tubs deserve their own section because the main danger is different. In a dry sauna, the biggest risks are fainting, falling, and overheating. In a hot tub, the biggest risk is drowning.

The water in most hot tubs is kept warm enough that your body can't easily shed heat, because you can't sweat into water the way you can into air. Your core temperature can rise steadily while you sit there feeling relaxed. Add alcohol and it's easy to get drowsy, nod off, or faint, and when that happens in water, your head can slip under quickly. Getting out is also the moment of highest fainting risk, because you're standing up from hot water onto wet, slippery steps.

Practical rules for hot tubs:

- **Don't drink in the hot tub.** That glass of wine or bottle of beer by the edge is the single biggest risk factor you can control.
- **Never use a hot tub alone after drinking**, and don't let a friend who has been drinking use one alone either.
- **Keep sessions short** and follow the temperature and time limits on the tub. Many manufacturers and safety agencies advise a maximum around 40°C (104°F).
- **Get out slowly.** Sit on the edge for a minute, then stand, holding a rail.
- **Glass and hot tubs don't mix** either. Broken glass in the water is hard to find and easy to step on.

## Steam Rooms, Infrared Saunas, and Cold Plunges

The same basic problem applies to other kinds of heat, with a few differences worth knowing.

**Steam rooms** run at a lower temperature than a dry sauna but with very high humidity. Because the air is already saturated, your sweat can't evaporate, so it cools you less. That means a steam room can feel milder while still raising your body temperature. The alcohol risks are the same: low blood pressure, dehydration, and dulled judgment.

**Infrared saunas** heat your body more directly and the air is usually cooler, so they can feel gentler. They still raise your heart rate and make you sweat. There's no good evidence that they're safe to use after drinking just because they feel less intense.

**Cold plunges and ice baths** after drinking bring a different set of risks. Sudden cold causes a gasp reflex and a sharp spike in heart rate and blood pressure, which is hard on a heart that alcohol is already pushing. Going from very hot to very cold quickly while drunk is the combination we'd most strongly avoid.

## The Next-Morning Sauna: Can You Sweat Out a Hangover?

This is one of the most common reasons people search for "sauna and alcohol," so it's worth being clear.

**You can't sweat out alcohol in any meaningful amount.** The vast majority of the alcohol you drink is broken down by your liver. Only a small fraction leaves through your breath, urine, and sweat. A sauna doesn't make your liver work faster, so it doesn't make you sober up sooner or clear alcohol from your body.

**A sauna also doesn't flush out the by-products that make you feel rough.** Your liver turns alcohol into acetaldehyde, a toxic compound linked to many hangover symptoms, and then into harmless acetate. That happens inside your liver cells, not in your sweat. There is no good evidence that sweating removes acetaldehyde or "detoxes" a hangover.

**It can make you feel worse.** A hangover often comes with some dehydration, a headache, and a tendency to feel lightheaded when you stand. A hot sauna adds more fluid loss and drops your blood pressure further. Some people do feel better afterwards, likely from relaxation and a warm, comfortable break, but that's a comfort effect, not a cure.

If you want to try it the next day:

- Wait until you're clearly sober, not just "probably fine."
- Drink water, ideally with some electrolytes, before you go in. Our guide to [rehydrating after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking) explains what actually helps.
- Keep it short and at a lower temperature than you'd normally choose.
- Skip it if you're vomiting, have diarrhea, feel dizzy, or have a pounding heart. Those are signs you're already low on fluid.
- Don't go alone.

We take a closer look at the whole "sweat it out" idea, including exercise and cold showers, in our guide to [whether exercise helps a hangover](/never-hungover/does-exercise-help-a-hangover).

## Who Should Be Especially Careful

For some people, the combination of heat and alcohol carries more risk than average. If any of these apply to you, it's worth talking to your doctor before mixing the two at all.

- **Heart conditions**, including coronary artery disease, heart failure, a past heart attack, or a known irregular heartbeat such as atrial fibrillation.
- **Low blood pressure or a history of fainting.** If you already get dizzy when you stand up quickly, heat and alcohol will make it worse.
- **High blood pressure, especially if treated with medication.** Many blood pressure medicines lower blood pressure further or affect how your body handles heat and fluid. Diuretics ("water pills") add to dehydration. Our guide to [alcohol and blood pressure](/never-hungover/alcohol-hypertension-blood-pressure-management-2025) covers how drinking affects blood pressure over time.
- **Diabetes.** Alcohol can lower blood sugar, and the symptoms of low blood sugar, such as shakiness, sweating, and confusion, are easy to mistake for simply being hot.
- **Epilepsy.** Heat, dehydration, poor sleep, and alcohol can all lower the threshold for seizures.
- **Pregnancy.** Hot tubs and saunas are generally advised against in pregnancy because of the risk of raising core body temperature, and alcohol isn't considered safe in pregnancy either.
- **People taking sedating medicines**, such as some antidepressants, anti-anxiety medicines, sleep aids, antihistamines, or opioid painkillers. These add to alcohol's drowsiness.
- **Older adults**, whose bodies tend to regulate temperature and blood pressure less well.

None of this means you can never use a sauna. It means the heat and the alcohol should be kept well apart, and your doctor is the right person to say how far.

## Warning Signs: When to Get Out, and When to Get Help

Get out of the heat straight away, sit or lie down somewhere cool, and drink water if you notice:

- Dizziness or lightheadedness, especially when you move
- Nausea
- A headache that's building
- A heartbeat that feels fast, pounding, or irregular
- Feeling unusually tired, weak, or confused
- Stopping sweating while you still feel very hot
- Muscle cramps

Lie down with your legs raised if you feel faint, rather than trying to walk it off. Most people recover within a few minutes once they're cool and lying flat.

**Call 911 (or your local emergency number) if** someone faints and doesn't come round within a minute or so, is confused or hard to wake, has chest pain or trouble breathing, has a seizure, has a very high body temperature with hot, dry skin, or was found under water in a hot tub, even if they seem to recover. Someone who has been very drunk and is now vomiting, breathing slowly, or can't be woken may have alcohol poisoning, which is a medical emergency in its own right. Keep them on their side and don't leave them alone.

## A Simple Plan for a Night That Includes Both

If your evening includes a sauna or hot tub and drinks, the order matters more than anything else.

1. **Heat first, drinks after.** Do your sauna or hot tub session while you're sober.
2. **Cool down fully.** Give yourself time to stop sweating and for your heart rate to settle.
3. **Rehydrate with water** before any alcohol. You've already lost fluid.
4. **Then have your drinks**, with food, and pace them.
5. **Don't go back in** once you've started drinking.

That one change, keeping heat and alcohol in separate parts of the evening, removes most of the risk.

## Where DHM Fits In

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound that some people take around drinking. Lab and animal research suggests it may affect how the body handles alcohol and may support the liver, and there's a small amount of human data. It's promising, but the evidence in people is limited. To be completely clear, **DHM does not make it safe to use a sauna or hot tub after drinking.** It doesn't stop alcohol from lowering your blood pressure, dehydrating you, or affecting your judgment, and there's no good evidence it reduces the risks covered in this article.

If you're interested in DHM for the rest of your night out, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. The things that actually make a sauna safe are the boring ones: be sober, stay hydrated, keep it short, and don't go in alone.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is it safe to go in a sauna after drinking alcohol?**

It isn't a good idea while you're still feeling the alcohol. Heat and alcohol both lower blood pressure and dehydrate you, and alcohol dulls the signals that tell you to get out, which raises the risk of fainting, falls, overheating, and heart rhythm problems. Wait until you're fully sober, drink water first, keep the session short, and don't go in alone.

**How long after drinking can I use a sauna?**

There's no official waiting time. A practical guide is at least an hour for each standard drink, and longer after several drinks, because your liver clears alcohol at a fairly steady pace that heat can't speed up. After a big night, leave the sauna until the next day. If you still feel any effect from the drinks, wait longer.

**Can you sweat out alcohol in a sauna?**

No. The vast majority of alcohol is broken down by your liver, and only a small amount leaves through sweat, breath, and urine. A sauna doesn't make your liver work faster, so it won't sober you up or clear alcohol from your body any quicker, and the extra sweating can add to dehydration.

**Does a sauna help a hangover?**

There is no good evidence that a sauna treats a hangover. It doesn't remove alcohol or acetaldehyde, the by-product linked to many hangover symptoms. Some people feel more relaxed afterwards, but heat can worsen dehydration, headaches, and dizziness. If you try it, wait until you're sober, rehydrate first, keep it short and cooler than usual, and skip it if you're dizzy or vomiting.

**Is it dangerous to drink alcohol in a hot tub?**

Yes, it's one of the riskier combinations. Hot water raises your body temperature, alcohol makes you drowsy and lowers your blood pressure, and fainting or falling asleep in water can lead to drowning. US safety agencies warn against using hot tubs while drinking. Don't drink in the tub, never use one alone after drinking, and get out slowly.

**Why do I feel dizzy in the sauna after drinking?**

Both heat and alcohol widen your blood vessels, so more blood pools in your skin and legs and less reaches your brain. Add the fluid you lose through sweat and the extra urine alcohol causes, and your blood pressure can drop, especially when you stand. Get out, lie down somewhere cool with your legs raised, and drink water. If you faint and don't come round quickly, or have chest pain, get emergency help.

**Is a steam room safer than a sauna after drinking?**

Not really. Steam rooms run cooler, but the humid air stops your sweat from evaporating, so they cool you less effectively and can still raise your core temperature. The main alcohol risks, which are low blood pressure, dehydration, and poor judgment, are the same. The same rules apply: wait until you're sober and keep it short.

**Can I have a beer after the sauna?**

Many people do, and having a drink after you've fully cooled down and rehydrated with water is much safer than drinking between sauna rounds. The main thing is the order: finish your heat sessions first, drink water, then have your drink, and don't go back into the sauna once you've started drinking.
